Turn 21 · Two things I left as links

“Write this one” went nowhere, and the badges on two profiles were words I made up.

Both are the same kind of omission: a button that implies a system nobody specified. The Almanac has three places that invite you to write an entry and no screen behind any of them. And two frames showed earned tags reading County Pilgrim · 50, Early Bird, The Classics and Trusted Seller — placeholders that sound like a phone game, one of them carrying a numeric tier, and none meaning anything a collector would recognise. Both frames now draw from the set below. Below: the submission flow, and thirteen badges with the exact rule for each.

21a

Write an Almanac entry

a form with the shape of the article, not a blank page
The Almanac › Write an entry Draft saves as you type
Anyone can write one. You own 41 Cameron County licences, which is why Cameron is the county suggested to you. Your holding appears under your name whatever you write about — a reader’s only way to weigh what you say.
What are you writing about
A county An era One licence type One particular licence Anything else
Cameron County, Pennsylvania▾
Nineteen counties are already written. The other forty-eight are open. The first four attach the entry to a county, an era, a type or a single item, so it turns up beside them everywhere on the site. Anything else attaches to nothing — deer camp, a warden’s notebook, how your grandfather stored his. Those live in the Almanac index only, and they’re the ones people will actually read for pleasure.
A picture for the top
Drop a photograph or choose a file
Runs full width above the title. Landscape, and it should be a licence or the ground itself rather than a portrait. Leave it empty and we use the best photograph from your own items for whatever you’re writing about, credited to you. Nothing is stock and nothing is generated.
It’s mine to publish
The one thing a reader should take away
Fewer than nine hundred residents took a licence here in 1926, which is why a complete Cameron run is the thing serious collectors quietly compete over.
This becomes the standfirst, in Petrona, above the body. One or two sentences. 168 / 300
The entry
Cameron was carved out of Clinton, Elk, McKean and Potter in 1860 and has never held more than six thousand people. The county issued its own numbered tags from 1913…
Plain paragraphs. No headings to choose — the layout supplies them.
What to look for — up to three
1
The 1926 trapper tags were hand-numbered. A printed number is a reproduction.
2
Add another thing to check
These become the boxed list. It’s the part people come back to, so it’s a separate field rather than something you have to remember to write.
Where you know this from
Game Commission annual reports, 1924–1931. My own forty-one. Two conversations with the county treasurer’s office.
Not published. It’s what a moderator reads to decide, and what a future correction gets checked against.
Send it for review Save the draft A moderator reads it within a week. You’ll get a letter either way.
What happens to it
1
A moderator reads it Against the sources field and the writer’s holding. Two outcomes only: publish, or send back with a note. No silent rejection.
2
It publishes under their name With their collection size and how long they’ve collected, as in 12b. The numbers panel and the live-listings rail attach automatically.
3
Corrections come in against it The author sees them first and can accept in one tap, which credits the corrector on the entry. Only a disagreement reaches a moderator.
An entry is never anonymous and never staff-written without a name on it. If nobody will put their name to a claim about a county, it shouldn’t be in the Almanac.
Why the form is this shape

A rich-text box gets you one long undifferentiated paragraph from a seventy-year-old collector who knows more about Cameron County than anyone alive. Asking for the takeaway, the body, the three things to check and the sources separately gets you the article in 12b without asking anyone to think about layout. It also means every entry looks the same without a house style guide.

The offer matters more than the form. Nobody browses looking for a writing job — so the invitation appears on the county page they’re already reading, when they own more of it than the average.
21b

Thirteen badges

each one a fact, with the query that proves it
Five kinds, thirteen badges no badge is awarded for spending money
Ground covered — needs CollectionSet
Run complete Any set with a rule reaches 100%. Names the set: Cameron 1913–1974, complete. The only badge that can be earned more than once.
All sixty-seven One licence from every issuing unit in a state, any year, any type. Reads All 67 counties in PA and All 64 parishes in Louisiana. The rarest one on the site.
The first decade Ten or more items from a state’s first ten years of issuing — 1913 to 1922 in Pennsylvania, read from licensing_start_year everywhere else. Depth in the era everyone finds hardest, rather than volume.
Year one Owns an item dated to a verified first-issue year. Names it: Year one · PA Elk, 2001. Reads State.min_license_year with its min_year_confidence and min_year_source — research already sitting in your reference data. Only awarded where confidence is high.
Across the line Items from three or more states. Most collectors never leave their own — and a non-resident licence is the thing that tempts them out.
Put something in — needs the Almanac
Wrote the entry One published Almanac entry. Names it: wrote Cameron County. This is the badge worth having, and the reason the flow in 21a exists.
Set it straight Five accepted corrections to entries you didn’t write. The quiet contributor’s badge — most knowledge arrives this way, not as whole articles.
Dealt straight — buildable today
Twenty-five clean Twenty-five completed orders with no live strike. Lapses the day a strike lands and returns when it expires.
Ships quick Median time to first tracking event under two days across the last ten orders. Rolling, so it can be lost by getting slow.
Traded true Ten trades where both sides confirmed receipt. Trades are the highest-trust thing on the site and nothing currently recognises them.
Knows the material — needs the questions
Thirty days A thirty-day streak on the three questions. Kept permanently once reached — it records something you did, not something you are.
Top of the board Finished a month in the top ten. Names the month.
Was here early — buildable today
Early season One of the site’s first hundred accounts. Nothing to do with activity, just when you showed up — and the only badge that can never be earned again once the hundredth account exists.
How they sit on a profile
Walt Brennan Cameron County · 412 items · since 1978
Wrote Cameron County Cameron run complete Twenty-five clean and 3 more
Three at a time, in that order — contribution, then ground covered, then conduct. The rest behind a count, because thirteen chips in a row is a games console and reads as noise rather than standing.
A rule of mine I need to take back

The settings pane says “tags are earned, not chosen — they appear on their own and never come off”. The first half is right and the second half can’t be, because three of these badges are statements about how somebody deals now.

A seller with twenty-five clean sales who then fails to ship must not keep a badge that says he’s reliable. So: a badge that records something you did is permanent, and a badge that describes how you are lapses when it stops being true. Nothing announces a lapse and nothing appears on the timeline — it simply isn’t there.

The copy in settings needs to say that instead. Everything else about badges being unchoosable stays.
Four tests each of these passes A collector would say it out loud. Nobody says “I’m a County Explorer”. Somebody would absolutely say they have a complete Cameron run. It’s one query. No scoring, no points, no tiers. If it needs a formula to explain, it’s a leaderboard, not a badge. Money can’t buy it. Nothing rewards spend, listing count, or sale value — the wealthiest member should not automatically be the most decorated. It helps somebody decide. Every badge answers either “should I trade with him” or “does he know what he’s talking about”. A badge that answers neither is decoration.

Correction to 17a

I badged the whole reports queue as needing a model. That was half wrong. MessageReport exists and is complete — reporter, reason, status, the conversation and the message, with resolve, dismiss and mark-reviewing actions.

What doesn’t exist is a report about a listing or an order — the reproduction-sold-as-original case, and condition-not-as-described. Those were two of the three rows I drew, and the reporting flow in turn 9 has nowhere to write to.

Cheapest fix is to widen MessageReport into a Report with a nullable listing and order alongside the existing conversation and message, keeping its status vocabulary — which is already the best of the four.
Two smaller ones, no frame needed
MarketplaceSettings deserves a screen, not a changelist It’s a singleton — you correctly refuse adds — holding platform_fee_percent and trade_label_fee_amount. Editing it as one row in a list of one hides the fact that changing a fee affects every live listing and every auction mid-flight. It wants a page that says how many, and asks whether the change applies to listings already running.
PrefillCorrection is a better signal than the tier table It records field_name, tier, was_accepted and was_cleared per field — which is what members actually did with our guess, not how confident we were. A high-tier guess that gets cleared is the most damning number you can collect, and it isn’t on the analytics page. Put cleared-rate beside each row in 17b.
What I’d leave alone

Shipments with events inline, trade offers with their items inline, bids and transactions read-only, notifications with their preview column, the State admin with license types and geographic units inline — all of these are the right shape already and a custom screen would be worse. Taxonomy needs the one thing in 17b and nothing else: ReferenceDataSuggestion already has accept-and-apply, which is the whole job.

Turn 18 · Three defects in what’s built

Two silent failures in the browse filters, and one constraint missing from the field that suspends people.

Not design work — these are things I hit while reading the code for turns 13, 14 and 17. None is urgent enough to stop anything, and each is a small change. Written up here so they don’t live only in a chat message.

18a

The three

two in browse_collections.html, one in enforcement/models.py
1 · The filter bar can empty itself and say nothing templates/collections/browse_collections.html · state change handler
What happens Changing the state clears the county select and all six license-type selects first, then fetches replacements from /api/geo-units/ and /api/license-types/ inside a bare Promise.all. There’s no catch. If either request fails — offline, 500, a slow connection at a show — the clearing has already happened and nothing arrives to replace it.
What the member sees A county dropdown containing only “Any” and six license-type triggers all reading “Any”, in a state that definitely has counties. No error, no spinner, nothing in the page to suggest a retry would help. The reasonable conclusion is that the state has no data and the site is broken.
The fix Fetch first, clear second — only replace the options once both responses are in hand. On rejection, restore the previous state selection and put one line under the bar: couldn’t load counties for Colorado. Try again. A disabled select with a reason beats an empty one without.
2 · The multi-select panel doesn’t follow the page same file · buildMultiSelect
What happens The panel is appended to document.body and positioned once from the trigger’s getBoundingClientRect plus scroll offset. Nothing recalculates it. Scroll, resize, or scroll the horizontal .filter-scroll strip and the panel stays where it was drawn while its trigger moves away.
Why it matters more than it looks There are six of these side by side in a strip that scrolls sideways on any narrow window, so this is the normal case rather than a corner. A checkbox list floating over unrelated rows, still live and still writing to a hidden select, is worse than a misaligned menu — you can tick the wrong filter without knowing which one you touched.
The fix Cheapest: close the panel on scroll and resize, as it already does on outside click and Escape. Better: drop the body append and use an absolutely positioned child of the filter item with position: relative on the wrapper, so it moves with its trigger for free.
3 · A strike can be excused with nobody recorded as having agreed apps/enforcement/models.py · Strike
What’s missing is_excused is a plain boolean, and excuse_reason, excuse_initiated_by, excuse_confirmed_by and excuse_confirmed_at are all independently blank or null. Nothing at the database level stops a row that is excused with an empty reason and no confirmer, or an unexcused row that carries a confirmation.
Why this field specifically It’s the field that decides whether somebody is suspended from selling. An excused strike doesn’t count toward the threshold, so a half-written excuse silently keeps a seller trading — and because the moderator screen reads the same booleans, it will display an excuse that nobody can be shown to have agreed to. That’s the one record you may later need to defend.
The fix A CheckConstraint: either is_excused is false and all five excuse fields are empty, or it’s true and reason, initiated_by, confirmed_by and confirmed_at are all present. Then the boolean is derivable rather than authoritative, and the audit trail can’t be partial.
One thing the first two have in common: both fail by showing a plausible-looking interface rather than an error. That’s the same rule as the empty states in 16b — never render a control over nothing. An empty select and an empty filter sidebar are the same bug in two places.
Turn 17 · The staff desk

You have sixteen admin changelists and no front door.

Django admin is the right tool for editing a row and I’m not replacing it — every list_display and list_filter in those sixteen files stays exactly as it is. What’s missing is the screen a moderator opens at nine in the morning, which has to answer one question: what will get worse if I don’t touch it today. So this is a queue desk, ordered by consequence, and it links out into the admin you already have. Deliberately a different colour from the member site — nobody should ever be unsure which one they’re looking at.

What you can do, and what each one does to him
Let it land Second live strike. He keeps selling. The buyer is refunded automatically and the item relists if he asks.
Hold 48 hours Sends him one more letter saying a strike is 48 hours away. Nothing else changes. Use this when somebody has a clean record.
Excuse it Needs a reason and the buyer’s confirmation. Neither exists here — the buyer said he’d wait, which isn’t the same as agreeing a delay.
Every one of these writes a Strike row with excuse_initiated_by set to you, so the audit trail says who decided and when.

The pattern, so the other thirty match

Every empty screen on the site is one of three shapes. Nothing yet — a Petrona sentence naming what will be here, one dark button, and where possible a real number from the database so the page isn’t hypothetical. Nothing matched — the filters shown as removable chips, then each relaxation with its own count, then the option to keep the search and be told later. Nothing left to do — green rule, plain statement, and a short list of what’s running so it reads as calm rather than broken.

Two things never to do Don’t render an empty control — a filter sidebar over nothing, a sort dropdown over zero rows, a matrix with no cells filled. Hide them until there is something to act on. And don’t use the word empty, or none, or zero, in anything a member reads.
Turn 15 · On a phone

Two things happen on a phone and nothing else: you get a letter and bid, or you’re at a show with a licence in your hand.

The desktop screens are for an evening at a desk — the matrix, the sets, nine settings rooms. None of that needs to shrink. What has to work on a phone is the auction clock and the camera, because a collector standing at a table at a gun show needs to know within ten seconds whether he already owns this and what it’s worth. Six screens, 390 points wide, every target at least 44.

What the phone drops

The matrix, the sets panel, the display case editor, the nine settings rooms, the Almanac article layout and the trade board’s dual rosters are all desk work. On a phone they become a single line that says “open this on a computer” rather than a cramped version nobody uses. The four tabs are Hunt, Mine, Bench and Add — the Almanac lives under Mine, because on a phone nobody browses reading matter, they arrive at it from a link in a letter.

The one screen that justifies an app

The camera answering “do I own this, and what’s it worth” in two taps is the only thing here a website can’t do as well. It needs the photo prefill you already planned, the comparable-sales figures from Price History, and nothing else. Everything on that screen is a read — no account required to try it, which makes it the best possible thing to put in front of somebody at a show who has never heard of the site.

Turn 14 · Fifty states, one interface

The word “county” is a Pennsylvania fact, not a product fact.

GeographicUnit already handles this properly and the design hadn’t caught up. Three things in the model break a county-shaped interface: units that are numbered rather than named (Colorado issues by GMU 12, not by Mesa), licences issued statewide with no unit at all, and units where geo_data_complete is false, so there is no shape to draw on a map. Pennsylvania is is_primary_default and stays the default everywhere. Nothing below is a new screen — it’s the same components under three conditions.

The rule for every screen already drawn

No screen in turns 1 to 13 needs redrawing. Four substitutions cover all of them: the field label and every sentence that says “county” come from issuance_unit_label; numbered units sort by unit_number and print with their type prefix; is_statewide renders as the word Statewide wherever a unit name would go; and anything that draws a shape checks geo_data_complete first and falls back to the matrix.

One thing the model can’t answer yet A set rule that says “every unit in this state” needs to know how many units existed in a given year, not how many exist now. GeographicUnit has no valid-from or valid-to. Until it does, a Colorado collector’s “19 of 185” is measured against today’s map, which will quietly overstate their gaps.
Turn 13 · Collectors

Browse Collections browses items. Nobody wants an item from a stranger — they want to know who has the rest.

What’s in browse_collections.html today is a good item browse: search, collector username, state, county, six license-type categories, era, year range, sort. That view stays, because it’s how you find one specific tag. But it can’t answer the question the zone is named after — who collects what I collect, who owns what I’m missing, and which of them will trade. So Collectors gets two tabs, and people is the one that opens first.

What changed and what didn’t

Every filter your template has is still here. Three things changed. The six license-type categories were labelled with their database names — holder_eligibility, activity_scope, addon_type — and now read as questions a person would ask. What you’ve chosen shows as removable chips instead of living inside nine closed dropdowns. And Apply is gone: the grid updates as you go, which is what the multi-select panels already imply.

The item card keeps the owner Your card already ends with the owner’s name and a View profile button, which is the right instinct — it’s the seam between the two tabs. I kept it and dropped the favourite count, which tells a browsing stranger nothing.
One thing to settle before this is built

Your browse is state-aware — there’s a State select, and the county label comes from issuance_unit_label, so a Louisiana collector sees Parish. Everything else I’ve drawn across thirteen turns says Pennsylvania and says county.

That’s fine if PA is the launch state and the rest is plumbing for later. It is not fine if a Louisiana collector can sign up on day one, because the matrix, the map, the Almanac and every set rule would all be mislabelled for them.

Answered in 14a: both, with Pennsylvania as the default. The unit word is read from the state, and two model cases the copy ignored — statewide issuance and unmapped units — are drawn there.
Turn 12 · The Almanac

The Almanac is the only part of the site that’s worth reading when you have no money to spend.

It is also the only thing here that can be found by somebody who has never heard of you: an era guide is a page a person lands on from a search engine at eleven at night, having just found a tin of their grandfather’s licenses in a drawer. So every piece ends in the same two places — what these are worth, and who has one for sale. All copy below is placeholder standing in for a real writer; the structure is the design.

This month’s county

Cameron County: the smallest run in the state

Fewer than nine hundred residents took a licence in 1926, and the county has never issued more than four thousand in a year since. Which is why a complete Cameron run is the thing serious collectors quietly compete over — and why two of the six known 1926 trapper tags are on this site.

12b

One entry, and the three questions

an era guide that sells things, and the game as it’s actually played
The Almanac › Eras › 1913–1922

The first decade, and why so few are complete

Walt Brennan · 412 items, collecting since 1978 March 2026 · 9 min

A 1913 licence was two objects that had to stay together: a metal button worn on the coat, and a paper tag that carried the number. Almost nobody kept both.

The button was the part a warden could see at forty yards, so it lived outdoors for a season and came home scratched. The tag was folded into a pocket, got wet, and was thrown out at the end of the year because it had expired. When a hunter died and his coat went to a jumble sale, the button went with the coat.

This is the whole reason the first decade is priced the way it is. A 1913 button on its own is a common object — there are eleven on this site today, and one will cost you sixty dollars. A 1913 button with its matching numbered tag is a different thing entirely, and the last one to sell here went for four hundred and ten.

What to look for
The numbers must match. Button and tag were issued as a pair. A mismatched pair is two items sold together, not one licence, and should be priced that way. Pin, not glue. The original fastening is a bent steel pin. A soldered or glued replacement is common and knocks a grade off. Read the county line. Nine counties abbreviated their name in 1913 and spelled it out from 1914, which dates an undated tag to the year.
Fourteen from this era are for sale now two are complete pairs

1915 Potter, tag only $74 · buy it now

Nine counties abbreviated in 1913 and spelled the name out from 1914 on. A five-figure serial rules out the small counties, and the tag stock changed in 1923 — so 1917 is the only year that fits all three.

Where the questions come from

Every question is generated from a real item in somebody’s collection with the identifying field hidden, and every explanation links to the Almanac entry that covers it. That means the game costs nobody any writing, gets harder as the site grows, and teaches the thing that makes people better buyers. It also lives on the home page as its own block — the Almanac is where the streak and the board live.

Turn 11 · The two things you can start

A set is what you’re building. A want is what you’re missing. Both were buttons with nothing behind them.

One naming decision first, because two things were both called a collection. My collection is everything you own — one page, all 412. A set is a named group inside it: the 1913–1930 residents, the north-central counties, the trapper licenses. Collectors already say set and run, so the word costs nothing to learn. If you’d rather it were group or folder, it’s one find-and-replace and the design is unchanged.

Why a rule and not just a folder

A folder is a filing cabinet: you put things in it and it does nothing else. A rule is a target — it knows what belongs, so it can count what’s missing, feed the matrix in 10b, seed the wanted list, and tell you that a gap came up for sale. The same panel does both; the rule is just the version that keeps working after you close it.

Three sets ship as suggestions Every collector gets offered the same three on their first visit, because they are what almost everyone is actually building: one from every county, a run of years for my county, and the first decade, 1913–1922. Accepting one is a single tap and it starts already half-full.

A want is a search, a signal, and a price ceiling

Those are three features your plan lists separately — saved searches, the public wanted list, and offer thresholds. One record does all three, so a collector fills in one form instead of three. The ceiling is the part that stays private: it decides whether you get a letter, and it never appears on your profile or to a trader.

What this needs from the model A WantedItem with county, year or decade or range, type, minimum grade, repairs-ok, ceiling, note, and two booleans for notify and publish. The set in 11a needs CollectionSet with a name, a nullable rule, and a membership table for hand-picked ones.
Turn 10 · My collection

The collection is the reason they joined. Today it reads like a spreadsheet with a photo column.

Everything in my_collection.html is here — the display case, the filter sidebar, the group-by, the item rows, the wanted list — but the order is wrong. A collector opens this page to answer one of three questions: what have I got, what am I missing, and what can I move. So the case sits at the top, the gaps get their own tracker, and the wanted list comes up out of the page footer where nobody scrolled to it.

Turn 9 · Letters, questions, and the map

The letters are the product for most of your members.

A collector who visits twice a week gets six emails in between. Right now those are the weakest thing you send: a generic wrapper that prints an enum label as a heading and pastes notification.message under it, or a bare page with a link to the dashboard. Nobody who receives one knows what to do without opening the site and going looking. Also in this turn: questions on a listing, writing a review, reporting and appealing, a lot listing, and the national map at size.

One shell, seven letters

Green bar, the mark, the date, a serif headline, an optional item block, one action, then a footer that says why it arrived. The other three — sale made, payment received, auction ended unsold — are the same shell with a different headline and item block.

The headline is a sentence

Not “Outbid” or the enum label your generic template prints. A collector reading only the subject line and the first line should know the item, the number, and the clock. That’s the whole job of the letter.

Georgia, and no image that must load

Petrona won’t render in most mail clients, so the letters keep Georgia — the family your current templates already use, and the closest web-safe cousin. The item photograph is nice to have; nothing depends on it, and every letter reads with images off.

Two lines worth stealing

“Replies reach a person, not a machine” instead of do not reply. And on anything with a deadline, the consequence in plain words — which nobody wants over a forgotten evening. That sentence is the difference between a rule and a reminder.

Say what the next buyer would want to know. Keep people’s addresses and prices out of it.

Answers sit under questions

Today the seller’s reply is a separate paragraph beginning “Seller:” and an unanswered question just says “Awaiting seller response.” Indented under the question, with the seller marked in brass, a run of six questions stays readable — and an unanswered one is visibly waiting.

Send price talk to the offer

“Would you take $150” in a public thread undercuts the listing for everyone reading it. Hidden with a one-line explanation and a link to Make an offer is kinder than a Flag button, and it teaches the norm once instead of moderating it forever.

Reviews with a shape

Three bare radio buttons labelled Positive / Neutral / Negative give no sense of what the middle means. Each option gets a line describing the deal it fits, and the footer draws the line between a poor review and an actual complaint — which is the distinction your enforcement system depends on.

Non-county states — game units, management zones — draw as a grid of named blocks in the same shades rather than a polygon map. Your reference data already says which is which.
One map, two places

The same component sits small at the foot of the home page and full size as a Hunt tab. It replaces the per-browse map that never loaded — one surface to keep working instead of four.

Your counties, outlined

Fill shows what’s for sale; a brass outline shows what you already hold. The two together answer the only question a collector brings to a map: where can I buy something I haven’t got. Only my gaps makes that the whole view.

The panel is the click target

Hovering gives a tooltip; clicking fills the side panel with the county’s count, year span, what you hold there, and a way through to both the listings and the collectors. A map that only filters is a novelty — a map that tells you something is a tool.
9f

How the map should actually look

a specimen sheet — every value, drawn at size

The aim is an engraved survey map, not a web map: no tiles, no roads, no satellite. Flat parchment ground, hairline county borders, four steps of green, and type that looks set rather than rendered. Your existing D3 already uses the right two neutrals — #b0a88a for borders and #f0ede6 for empty — so this mostly formalises what’s there and fixes the ramp.

The ink

Nothing listed #F0EDE6
One #E8F5E2
Two to four #B9D6A8
Five to nine #7FAE6A
Ten to twenty-four #3F7A2C
Twenty-five and up #1A5C0D

Your code currently runs a continuous ramp — scaleSequential([0, max], interpolate('#e8f5e2', '#1a5c0d')) — so no two counties share a shade and the legend can never be honest. Quantise it into these five buckets on fixed counts, not on the maximum. Then Lycoming stays the same green whether the busiest county has 40 listings or 400, and the legend is a promise rather than a decoration.

A single county, in every state it can be

Specimens, not cartography — the real shapes come from TopoJSON
Lycoming
At rest Hairline #B0A88A at 0.5px. Label only if it has listings and the shape is wide enough.
Lycoming
Under the cursor Border thickens to 2px forest and the fill darkens a step. No lift, no shadow — paper doesn’t float.
Lycoming
You hold one from here Brass rule inside the border, 1.5px. It reads as a mark on the map rather than a change to it.
Cameron
Held, nothing for sale The common case, and the one a collector scans for: brass ring on empty ground.
Lycoming
Chosen Dark border plus a brass ring outside it, and the side panel fills. Only one at a time.

The tooltip

Lycoming County 86 listed · 1913–1979 You hold 14 from here Click to hunt it
Dark ground so it reads over any fill, three lines and a prompt, no arrow. It follows the cursor with a 12px offset and never crosses the edge of the frame. On a touch screen the first tap shows it, the second opens the county.

The type on it

Pennsylvania State name, Petrona 600, set once in the top-left of the frame.
Lycoming County labels, Public Sans 700 at 10px, 0.08em. Dark ink on the three pale fills, cream on the two dark ones.
86 Counts only appear above 40 listings — the shade carries the rest. Anything more is clutter at this size.
New York Neighbouring states: no fill, a 0.5px #DCD6C6 outline and a grey name. Context, not content.

Three depths, one component

the lower 48, state outlines only
no county lines at this depth
1 · The country States shaded by the same five buckets. Only the fourteen with reference data are clickable; the rest sit at 35% with no fill. Albers, not Mercator — Mercator makes a nonsense of the northern states.
one state, 67 counties
fitSize on the state’s own bounds
2 · The state The working view, and where a Pennsylvania collector should land by default. Counties fill the frame with a 16px margin; neighbours are drawn faintly beyond it so the shape is recognisable.
chosen county held dark
the panel does the talking
3 · The county No third zoom. Choosing a county keeps the state in view and fills the side panel — there is nothing below county level worth drawing, and pretending otherwise costs a tile server.

States without counties

Colorado · game management units
GMU 4 GMU 5 GMU 12 GMU 18 GMU 23 GMU 27 GMU 31 GMU 40 GMU 44 GMU 51
Same five shades, same brass ring, same tooltip. Ordered by unit number, wrapping to the frame — it stops being a map and becomes a table that behaves like one, which is honest.

Things not to do

No basemap. No roads, no terrain, no satellite. The moment a tile appears the page stops looking like a survey and starts looking like a delivery app. No pins. A license was issued by a county, not at a point. Filling the county is the truthful representation; a marker in the middle of Lycoming is a lie about precision. No animated draw-in. Sixty-seven paths easing in is a two-second toll on every visit. Render once, and hold. No shadow, no rounded corners, no gradient fill. Everything else on the page is flat ink on paper; the map is where that either holds or breaks. Never a dead end. An empty county still opens the panel — with what you hold there, who collects it, and an offer to save a hunt for it. Which is the one thing the current map, when it loaded, never did.
Turn 8 · The rest of My Bench

Five workspaces that were five separate pages nobody could find.

My listings is a stack of cards with a pipe-separated line of metadata. Favorites is two grids with an Unfavorite button under every tile. The notifications centre is a list where every row carries its own Mark read form. None of them shows a count, a filter, or what needs doing — and all five were reachable only through the username dropdown. As tabs of one workspace they can share a shape: a filter row, a table or list that answers “what needs me” first, and one action per row.

One page, one job

Eight cards become a header that says what this is, a five-stop rail that says where it is, and one brass-bordered box that says what to do. Everything else — money, addresses, the other party — is reference material and moves to the right. The Stripe session id goes; nobody has ever needed it.

Two ways to ship, side by side

Today the label button and the manual tracking form are stacked in a “Seller Shipping Actions” card with no explanation of the difference. Shown as a pair, with the price already covered on the left and “your own postage” on the right, the choice takes a second. The package inputs disappear entirely — they were captured on the listing.

The handshake, offered early

In the current page the exception flow only appears once a strike exists — after the damage. Offering it beside the deadline, in the seller’s own language, means the local-pickup and agreed-delay cases get settled before anyone is penalised. That is the difference between a rule and a fair rule.

The clock is the content

Every state says what happens if the buyer does nothing: cancelled in 24 hours, nothing to do, assumed arrived on Monday. Those numbers are your release_unpaid_auction_wins and auto_complete_orders defaults — 24 hours and three days — finally visible to the person they apply to.

Confirm receipt, asked properly

“Confirm receipt” is a form label, not a question. Did it turn up all right? gets a real answer, and it gives the unhappy buyer a door that isn’t silence — which is what you want before a dispute hardens. Positive / neutral / negative become Good / Middling / Poor; same three values in your Review model.

The collection card replaces a screen

Your green gradient banner sends the buyer to a separate add_from_order form to re-enter what the platform already knows. Since every listing now comes from a shelf item, the purchase simply lands on theirs — and the only thing worth asking for is what they paid and a private note.

Reasons as sentences

Your five excuse reasons are a <select> of enum labels — local_pickup, agreed_delay, combined_shipment. As five plain statements you pick from, a seller who is flustered can answer in one read. Same five values underneath.

Say what each button does

The confirming side currently gets one button reading “Confirm Handshake” with no statement of consequence. Spelling out both outcomes — and that declining is silent — is what makes people willing to answer honestly rather than ignore it, which is the failure mode that costs you a member.

The ladder, on the page

One strike, two, three — printed beside the flow that could produce one. Enforcement feels arbitrary when it’s invisible until it lands. Note the whole panel is written for someone who is probably annoyed: short sentences, no policy voice, and a way out at the bottom.
Turn 6 · Three steps, and every option panel

Pick where it’s going first. Then describe it. Then set the terms.

You’re right and 5a was wrong: the destination should be the first question, not the last. It’s the thing a seller already knows when they walk up, and asking it first lets the form tailor itself immediately. The “yours or stock” question is gone — it was solving a problem the destination choice solves better. Title and Description move to the top under their real names, condition gets its own written description, and the six taxonomy dimensions come out of the drawer.

Same shape, different questions

Each panel is short because it only carries its own fields — the current form holds all three sets at once and hides two with JavaScript. Each also ends with the same three things: the action, what it costs you to change your mind, and one line of local knowledge. Sunday evenings, comparable sales, the county gap it closes.

The collection panel is the interesting one

It asks nothing about money publicly and everything about privacy. Three of its controls exist today — is_public, trade_eligible and featured are all on CollectionItem. The folder needs 10.14, and the private block — what you paid, where you got it, a note to yourself — is three new fields I’m proposing, marked as such on the panel. That block is what makes cataloguing worth doing.

Selling from your collection skips step 2

Pick an item in 6a, confirm a two-line summary, and you land straight on one of these two selling panels with the photographs, county, year and condition already carried across. That is the whole point of the shelf being the source of truth — the second sale of a duplicate should take under a minute.
Turn 5 · One door, and the item form

One “Add an item.” Where it goes is a decision you make after the item exists, not before.

Your own plan already answers this and I don’t think you’ve noticed. 10.10 removes trade as a listing type, so there are only two marketplaces left to post to. 10.15 then says single-item listings keep the source_collection_item requirement, with lots as the explicit exception. Put those together and every single item on the site is already a collection item first, and a listing is something you do with one. So there is one add flow, and selling is a disposition — not a separate door with its own form.

5a

The entry-point question

Today — three doors, two forms, one weak bridge
Create Listing Config page: pick a marketplace, optionally pick a collection item → the big form
Add to Collection A second, nearly identical form on the profile
↓ and separately
Trade Not a door at all — starts from a collection item somebody already added
What it costs you: two forms with the same twenty fields, two prefill wirings, and the same license entered twice if you own it and then sell it. The bridge between them is one dropdown labelled “List from collection (optional)” sitting at the very top of the listing form, which is the least likely place anyone looks. It also produces the odd step you already have to carry: after an order completes, the buyer is offered a separate “add this to your collection” screen for an item the system has fully described.
Proposed — one door, then a disposition
+
Add an item One button, one form, one photo read. Everything starts here.
↓ It’s in your collection. Now what?
Keep it Nothing more to do. It shows on your profile.
Sell it at auction Start price, increment, how long it runs
Sell it at a price Your price, and whether you’ll take offers
Open it to trade What you’d want back, cash either way
The last three aren’t exclusive. A store item can take offers and trades — that’s the three buyer actions 10.10 specifies. Only auction is exclusive, because a live lot can’t be traded away underneath a bidder. And a disposition is reversible: end a lot, drop the price, close it to trade. The item survives all of it, because the item is the thing you own.

The dealer objection, which is real

Somebody flipping thirty licenses does not want stock showing up in their personal collection. Answer it with one question on the form — is this yours, or is it stock? Stock lives on the shelf, is never public, never counts toward county progress, and never appears on the profile. It is one boolean, and it is the difference between the collectors and the dealers being able to share a single flow.

What this deletes

The config page goes — nobody should pick a marketplace before they’ve described an item. The second collection form goes. The “List from collection” dropdown goes, because listing from your shelf is now the only way it works. And the post-order “add this to your collection” screen becomes one line on the order: this is on your shelf now.

The one exception

Lots. A box of forty 1950s licenses isn’t a collection item and shouldn’t become forty of them. 10.15 already treats lots as the exception to the source_collection_item rule, so keep a second, quieter entry — List a lot — under the same Add button. Two entries, not four, and the second one is rare by design.

What moved, and why

Today the form is one 960px column and the photo zone sits at the top, so every field is below the fold and the prefill results appear a long way from the fields they filled. Splitting it puts the evidence — the photograph, what was read off it, the resulting card — permanently on the left while you work down the right. Four collapsed <details> blocks in a row become one, because taxonomy is genuinely optional and shipping belongs in step 2 with the rest of the selling decisions.

The photo read-out is the new thing

You built a genuinely unusual feature and nothing on screen says so. A plain list of what it read, with a tick for confident, a question mark for check-this, a chip for take-it-or-leave-it, and one row for a word it couldn’t match, turns invisible cleverness into visible help. The unmatched row is also where “Is a value missing?” belongs — at the moment of the miss, not in a collapsed panel at the foot of the page.

Two smaller wins

The title writes itself from year, county, residency and attachments — the order collectors actually search in — with an escape hatch. And the completeness score stops being a number in a list of nineteen and becomes a line under the card that says what to add next. Errors keep your existing summary-at-top pattern, which is good; they just also mark the field and say what the bound is.

Why this beats the config page

Asking “which marketplace” first forces a decision before the seller has looked at the thing properly, and it can’t offer any help — there is no item yet, so no comparable sales, no fee estimate, no card to look at. Asking second lets the page do all three. And because only auction is exclusive, the choice stops being a fork and becomes a set of switches.

The three things a seller wants to know

What’s it worth, what will I keep, and who will see it. Comparable sales sit beside the price field, the fee breakdown is spelled out rather than discovered at payout, and the last card says two people are already waiting for this county and year. All three come from data you have.

The auction and trade panels

Not drawn here, but they are the same shape: pick the disposition, that panel opens with only its own fields — start price, smallest raise, how long it runs, reserve for auction; wanted-back notes and cash direction for trade — and the rail keeps showing the proceeds and the card. Shipping is shared, and comes from your defaults in every case.
Turn 4 · The door, and all ten settings rooms

Sign-in as an application form, and every settings tab drawn out.

The two auth pages are bare Django forms in a parchment card today — four unlabelled fields and a button. They’re also the first thing a collector ever sees, so they set the whole tone. Here they read like a membership application from a licence office: a ruled header with a form number, small-caps field labels, and one plain sentence explaining what each step is for. Sign-up also has to carry the versioned Terms acceptance your plan requires at 10.16, which nothing in the current form does.

The table

Inverting the middle two columns does three things at once: the licenses on the table become the brightest objects on the page, direction is carried by position and one brass arrow instead of red-versus-green, and the two halves finally read as one deal rather than two lists that happen to sit together. Cash sits in a recessed strip at the foot of each side — lit when it’s in play, dim when it isn’t.

The rail is back

Negotiation history and the other trader’s card return to a full 300px rail, vertical timeline and all. It bought back its width from the rosters, which shrank to 196px picker lists — a 30×23 thumbnail and a truncated title is enough to recognise your own license, and the shelves are for finding, not admiring.

Three decisions, weighted

The action bar is now a light band under the dark table, so it separates cleanly, and it restates the terms in Petrona at 21px before the buttons. Review & accept is brass, 14px, with a raised edge; counter is outlined in forest; decline is the quietest thing there. Accept goes to the confirmation screen your plan already requires, never straight through.

What you have today

A gradient header with badges, a featured display case, two tabs, and a “Looking For” list rendered as bare sentences at the very bottom. Everything is present but flat — there is nothing to tell you whether this person is worth trading with, and no sense of what they actually collect.

What changed

Trust moves up beside the name as a card you can read in one glance, and the three actions sit under it. Tags from 13.b.4 land under the bio, where earned recognition belongs. Ground covered brings the 10.14 tracker onto the public profile, so the profile answers “what does he collect” visually. Captions on display-case pieces are the whole point of a display case — they turn inventory into a person.

The trade hook

The “looking for” rail is cross-referenced against your own collection — you have one, 1931, mint. That single line is the difference between a profile you read and a profile you act on, and it needs no new models: it is the wanted-list matcher from 10.14 pointed at one user instead of new listings.

What’s there today

One 720px column, six stacked cards, no navigation: Account readiness, Profile details (display name, county, bio, avatar), Email verification, Shipping addresses, Listing defaults (carrier, who pays, package dims, bid increment, auto-relist), Blocked users. It is honest and it works — the problem is that it is the only place any preference lives, so it will keep growing downward until nobody can find anything.

Two things to fix regardless of layout · UserProfile.county is a free-text CharField while listings use a GeographicUnit FK. That is why the profile shows “Towson, MD, PA” class bugs. Point it at the same reference data. · Account readiness lists “Phone verified” with no way to do it. Either ship the 10.12 flow or don’t show the row — an unreachable requirement reads as a broken site.
The ten rooms
Profile & display — name, home county (as a real FK), bio, portrait, plus which of the four showcase layouts the public profile uses (10.14). Verification & trust — email, the phone OTP flow, and a plain statement of what each unlocks. Trading needs phone; selling needs an address. Addresses — the existing book, unchanged. Alerts & saved hunts — new. Saved searches, wanted list, and per-event delivery. The single biggest return lever you have. Notifications & mail — the 10.13 preference model, with mandatory categories shown as locked rather than hidden. Listing defaults — today’s card, plus “allow offers” and “open to trade” as defaults now that both exist. Payouts & fees — Stripe connection state and the fee schedule, read-only. Sellers ask; nothing in the app answers. Privacy & blocking — blocked users, whether the collection and wanted list are public, whether the county shows. Records & export and Policies & standing — the 10.18 twelve-month CSV, and the ToS version accepted plus any strikes with the appeal link. Standing belongs somewhere calm and private, not on a dashboard.

Idea 8 · the live preview

On the create-listing page, pin the buyer’s card to the right of the form and update it as the seller types. It answers “is this good enough to post” better than any completeness percentage, and it quietly teaches sellers that a photo and a county are what make a card work. The card component already exists — render it with the unsaved form values.

Turn 2 · Home page, masthead, trade board

Keep the three names. Take them out of the navigation and put them back where they belong — on the goods.

Turn 1’s shell was still a little app-shaped: 8–12px radii, soft drop shadows, sans-serif everywhere in the chrome. This pass tightens it into something pressed rather than rendered — 4px corners, hairline rules instead of shadows, letterspaced small caps for labels, tabular figures for anything numeric, and a broadsheet masthead on the home page that compresses to a single bar everywhere else.

Note 8 — why this reads better

The old bar had one weight of sans-serif at one size doing four different jobs, four equal-weight links floating in the middle, and a pill button. Here the hierarchy is material: nameplate in Petrona, nav in letterspaced small caps like pressed type, a brass hairline separating the eyebrow, an inset search well that looks recessed rather than floating, and square 3px corners. Nothing is centred for the sake of symmetry.

Notes 3 & 7 — trail and mail

The breadcrumb is worth it, with one change: make it the trail of the hunt you were on, not a static hierarchy. Every crumb carries your filters, and the last item is a plain-language way back (“Back to those 86 results”). On mail — a bare bell is a guess. Both trays get a word next to the glyph, brass for mail and rust for alerts, so unread mail is a labelled thing on the page rather than a dot you have to notice.

Note 5 — the three names

Keep them. Your own plan already settled it: 10.10 removes the separate Trading Block browse and keeps the name as the trade dashboard. Do the same for the other two — they stop being four indexes and become the three ways a deal happens. They label every card, they name the three doors on the home page, and The Trading Block names the negotiation workspace. A fourth nav item, The Almanac, is where the Education Hub, county spotlights and trivia eventually live — the room the brand is actually about.

Turn 1 · Recommendation

KeystoneBid doesn’t need four marketplaces. It needs one catalog, one workspace, and one shell.

The four pillars in the nav today are transaction formats, not places. A collector hunting a 1923 Lycoming County resident tag has to guess whether it lives in the Auction House, the General Store, or the Trading Block, then run the same filter bar three times. Meanwhile everything that belongs to them — bids, orders, listings, collection, favorites, messages — is stacked in an eleven-item username dropdown. That is the source of the siloed, disjointed feeling. Below: the structural fix, the shell every page inherits, and four screens built on it.

County numbers · 1913–1937

The twenty-four years Pennsylvania numbered its counties

Adams was 01 and York was 67, alphabetical and stable for the whole numbered era. When the quota ran out between 1920 and 1937 the Commonwealth printed un-numbered “Special Issue” tags instead — which is why a 1931 tag with no county number is not a fake.

Why this is engaging

Nothing here is decoration. Every band answers a question a collector actually has when they open the site: what closes tonight, what happened while I was out, what am I missing, what turned up, and where is the ground I don’t cover. The old page answered none of them.

The Day Book is the big one

Your idea file calls the activity feed the biggest missing engagement driver, and it’s right — but written as a ledger with the hour in the margin rather than a social feed, it reads like a shop’s day book instead of a timeline. It needs no new models: Notification, Bid, Listing.created_at and Shipment events already carry all six lines.

The Almanac earns the return visit

One researched note a week, ending in a link to the items it describes, is the cheapest engagement in the plan — and you have already paid for the research. That county-number entry is lifted from R1 in the prefill data plan. This is what makes the site feel like it belongs to people who care about the objects.

How four columns fit

Two things bought the room. The negotiation history moved out of a right rail and became a four-cell strip along the bottom — three versions and the current message read fine as a row. And the roster tiles are 36×28 thumbnails with two lines of text instead of cards, which is all you need to recognise your own licenses. Each column scrolls independently, so the board never grows past one screen.

What makes it fast

Both rosters are filtered by relevance, not alphabetically: my column defaults to Walt’s wants, his column defaults to my gaps. Items already on the table stay visible in the roster with a check so you never lose your place, and an item listed in the Auction House greys out with the reason — the is_tradeable rule from 10.10 shown rather than enforced silently. Cash sits in both middle columns because either side can offer it.

“Should trades be their own browse page?”

No. Trade availability is a property of an item, not a different kind of item — and plenty of sellers will take cash or a swap. Put Open to trade in the Hunt filter rail next to Bid and Buy now. Keep a Trading Block landing page as a marketing door and a place for the trade-specific tools (wanted-list matches, active negotiations), but never as a second index of licenses.

“Should collections go under profiles?”

Collections are one dataset with two doors. Managing yours is work, so it lives in My Bench with add / edit / visibility / trade-eligible controls. Looking at someone’s is discovery, so it lives on the collector profile under Collectors. Delete the standalone Collections browse tab; it competes with both.

“Where do orders, favorites, bids go?”

My Bench, as visible tabs. The dropdown is the reason nothing feels connected: it hides state. The most important tab is Needs you — every deadline the platform already tracks (pay by, ship by, confirm receipt, offer expires) surfaced as one list of actionable rows. That single page is what makes the three marketplaces feel like one product.

Parchment stops being the default card background — that’s what makes every page read as one flat beige mass today. White surfaces on a warm page, parchment reserved for grouping and quiet zones. Green gets darker so white text on it is comfortable; amber warms into brass and is used only for accents and one primary action per view.
